title: Original Art Show and Tell with David Choe
summary: A visual companion in which David Choe and a Felix Comic Art host move through original pages and paintings by Geof Darrow, Tradd Moore, Daniel Warren Johnson, Simon Hanselmann, Edvin Biuković, Ian Bertram, Frank Teran and Frank Quitely. Choe explains what he buys, why initial difficulty can deepen attachment, how he gives art to friends, why death changes his attention, and how direct criticism becomes friendship or attempted collaboration. The closing Frank Quitely piece becomes a literal Choe/Quitely collaboration when Choe paints over the original inks. Automatic captions badly damage nearly every artist and work name. Because the page on camera is often the evidence, uncertain object identities remain marked for frame verification rather than inferred from the audio.

connections.why: A channel appearance directly produces Choe's friendship and possible collaboration with Geof Darrow.
Choe frames specific criticism as more useful than undifferentiated praise, echoing the demanded-praise conflict in the 2026 Bobby/Oliver film.
The request for a minimal panel reveals a compositional principle: intensity needs contrast.
Frank Miller, Luther Strode and other initially inaccessible work become the art he values most.
Collecting becomes an extension of repeated attempts to write for an admired artist.
The side-by-side Tradd Moore pages support a concrete account of stiff detail developing into organic psychedelia.
Seeing the physical page corrects assumptions about drawing size and labor.
The shown page operationalizes the same quiet/loud contrast Choe asked Darrow to explore.
The page attaches Choe's ownership and visual response to a stable creative object.
Food dye matters as making-process evidence, not decorative trivia.
Choe describes collecting as circulation among friends rather than only possession or investment.
A direct art-for-art trade explains provenance without exposing a private collector.
The speaker openly examines why death intensifies his attention to art and music.
Researching a nearly forgotten Punisher run before broadcast shows how coverage can change collector demand.
The episode's subject reportedly contacts Choe after the Kayfabe feature, turning archival attention into a current relationship.
The final object connects an unpublished story experiment, The Choe Show marketing and Choe painting directly over Quitely's inks.

source_notes.claim: Tradd Moore created Luther Strode and The New World.
source_notes.assessment: Image Comics lists Moore as artist and co-creator of both works. Exact pages shown still require frame-level object verification.

source_notes.claim: The displayed Daniel Warren Johnson page belongs to Wonder Woman: Dead Earth.
source_notes.assessment: DC confirms Johnson wrote and drew the four-part Black Label series. The transcript names the work; the individual page needs visual comparison.

source_notes.claim: Frank Teran drew The Punisher #94 and #95.
source_notes.assessment: The 1994 issue records credit Frank Teran as artist on the two-part No Rules story. The Pulp Fiction comparison remains Choe's interpretation.

speaker_policy.reason: The source contains at least David Choe and a Felix Comic Art host, with overlap and camera-dependent object reference. Participant names may index the work, but no listening-verified turn boundaries or held-out acoustic identity windows exist.

Do not choose a cause of Edvin Biuković's death from the speaker's contradictory uncertainty.
Do not identify the damaged third performer name or surface the passage as erotic discovery content.
